question.text: The principle of "Utmost Good Faith" (Uberrimae Fidei) in insurance places a duty on which party to disclose all material facts?

answer.text: Only the insurer must disclose all policy terms
The insured must disclose all relevant information to the insurer
The insurance agent must disclose all competitors' products
Both insurer and insured share equal duty, but neither can reject claims for non-disclosure

explanation.text: The Logic: Per NISM Series X-B (p.21), the principle of utmost good faith places the obligation on the insured to disclose all relevant information truthfully to the insurer. The source states that if material information is suppressed, the insurer has the right to reject the claim. Per p.28, the workbook also advises full disclosure while taking an insurance policy, reinforcing the same obligation. The Trap: Option D is close but wrong on the consequence — the insurer can reject claims for non-disclosure by the insured, so the duties are not symmetric. Option A inverts the obligation onto the insurer. Option C describes a marketing/comparison duty, not the utmost-good-faith principle. Note: The right of the insurer to reject a claim for material non-disclosure is the load-bearing consequence the source attaches to this principle.
